original_question: Given a Diophantine equation, either list all its integer solutions or prove that it has infinitely many integer solutions.
target_in_paper: Problem 1 (the finiteness problem), specialized in the current project to the nine unresolved equations of size H ≤ 24 listed in Table 1; concretely, the paper's sharpened challenge is: prove that every equation in Table 1 has infinitely many integer solutions. citeturn28view0citeturn28view1
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the paper's core finite-versus-infinite dichotomy for integer solution sets: if the set is finite, one should determine all integer solutions, while if it is infinite, a proof of infinitude suffices. This is exactly the logic behind the paper's finiteness problem. citeturn27view1turn28view0
missing_details: The paper is not asking about an arbitrary Diophantine equation in full generality; its concrete open problem concerns the nine specific equations listed in Table 1.
The ambient domain must be stated explicitly: the variables are integer variables, i.e. (x,y,z) ∈ Z^3.
The official formulation is the finiteness problem: determine whether the set of integer solutions is finite or infinite; only in the finite case must all integer solutions be listed.
The equations are selected by the paper's size ordering H(P) = Σ |a_i| 2^{d_i} for a reduced polynomial P, and Table 1 contains exactly the equations of size H ≤ 24 for which Problem 1 remains open.
The nearby structural reformulation is missing: all nine equations have the form z^2 + (y^2 + a)z + P(x) = 0 with a ∈ Z and P(x) a cubic polynomial.
The paper's sharp current target is stronger than the draft's generic wording: it explicitly proposes proving that every one of the nine Table 1 equations has infinitely many integer solutions.
An explicit equivalent reformulation is omitted: for each listed equation, one can ask whether the discriminant (y^2 + a)^2 - 4P(x) is a perfect square for infinitely many integer pairs (x,y).
refined_question: Solve the finiteness problem for the nine polynomial Diophantine equations in integers x, y, z listed in Table 1 of arXiv:2404.08518, namely: z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 - 2 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 - x - 1 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 + x - 1 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 + x + 1 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 - 3 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 + 3 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 - x - 2 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z + x^3 - x + 2 = 0; z^2 + y^2 z - z + x^3 + 2 = 0. That is, for each equation determine whether its integer solution set is finite or infinite, and, in the precise sharpened form proposed in the paper, prove that each of these nine equations has infinitely many integer solutions. citeturn28view0turn28view1
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for each of the nine equations written in the form z^2 + (y^2 + a)z + P(x) = 0 with a ∈ Z and P(x) a cubic polynomial, prove that the discriminant (y^2 + a)^2 - 4P(x) is a perfect square for infinitely many integer pairs (x,y). citeturn28view2
justification: The draft is pointing at the project's finiteness problem rather than at the harder task of fully parametrizing every infinite solution set. In the surrounding project literature, this is formulated as deciding whether the integer solution set is finite and, if so, listing all solutions; the author also states that proving infinitude already completely resolves that problem. The current arXiv:2404.08518 update then narrows this general framework to the nine explicit size-H ≤ 24 equations in Table 1 and states the concrete challenge to prove that all nine have infinitely many integer solutions. That is the closest sharp, stand-alone, paper-faithful refinement of your draft. citeturn27view1turn28view0turn28view1
